what.body:
Trees describe hierarchies, but your own life is full of networks, such as friends and roads, and a graph is how we write them down. Trees describe hierarchies; graphs describe anything connected. Road maps (cities joined by roads), the internet (routers joined by links), social networks (people joined by friendship), a circuit (components joined by wires), the prerequisites of courses (course A must precede B) are all graphs. A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices (nodes) V and a set of edges E, each edge joining two vertices. Edges may be undirected (a road you can drive both ways) or directed (a one-way street, “A must precede B”), and may carry a weight (distance, cost, capacity).

The vocabulary again. Two vertices joined by an edge are adjacent. In an undirected graph the degree of a vertex is the number of edges at it; the handshake lemma says the degrees sum to twice the number of edges, because each edge has two ends. In a directed graph a vertex has an in-degree and an out-degree. A path is a sequence of vertices with an edge between each consecutive pair; its length is its number of edges (or the sum of the weights). A cycle is a path that returns to its start. A graph is connected if a path joins every pair of vertices; otherwise it splits into connected components. A tree is a connected graph with no cycles — exactly n − 1 edges. A DAG is a directed acyclic graph. A graph with few edges (E ≈ V) is sparse; one with many (E ≈ V²) is dense, and a complete graph has every pair joined (n(n − 1)/2 edges).

Pick one network from your life, such as the bus routes you use, and decide whether its edges are directed, undirected or weighted.
keynotes: A graph G = (V, E) is a set of vertices and a set of edges, each edge joining two vertices.
Edges may be undirected (a two-way road) or directed (a one-way street), and may carry weights.
Road maps, the internet, social networks, circuits and course prerequisites are all graphs.

rep.body:
There are two standard ways to hold a graph in memory, and they trade space against speed in a way you can predict. How do we put a graph in memory? The two standard answers trade space against speed. The adjacency matrix is a V × V table A where A[i][j] = 1 (or the weight) if there is an edge i → j and 0 otherwise; an undirected graph gives a symmetric matrix. Testing whether two vertices are adjacent is O(1), but the table needs V² cells whatever the number of edges, and listing a vertex’s neighbours costs O(V). The adjacency list keeps, for each vertex, a list of its neighbours (with weights); it needs only V + 2E entries (V + E for directed graphs), listing the neighbours of v costs only deg(v), and testing a particular edge costs O(deg).

Choose by density. Real-world graphs — road networks, the web, a social network — are sparse (each vertex touches a handful of others), so adjacency lists are the default and make the traversal algorithms run in O(V + E). The matrix wins for dense graphs, for algorithms that ask “is there an edge?” constantly, and for the matrix-multiplication-style algorithms (Floyd–Warshall). An edge list (a plain array of (u, v, w) triples) is the natural input for Kruskal’s algorithm.

For a graph with 1000 vertices and only 2000 edges, which representation would you pick, and why?
keynotes: The adjacency matrix is a V × V table that needs V² cells whatever the number of edges, and tests adjacency in O(1).
The adjacency list keeps for each vertex a list of its neighbours and needs only V + 2E entries.
Sparse graphs favour lists and dense graphs favour matrices.

bfs.body:
Imagine dropping a stone in a pond: the ripples spread outwards one ring at a time, and that is breadth-first search. To explore a graph from a start vertex s, you need a rule for what to do next. Breadth-first search (BFS) visits s, then all of s’s neighbours, then all their unvisited neighbours, and so on — expanding like ripples in a pond. The tool is a queue: mark s visited and enqueue it; repeatedly dequeue a vertex u, process it, and for each unvisited neighbour v, mark it visited and enqueue it. Marking on enqueue (not dequeue) prevents a vertex from being added twice. Each vertex enters the queue once and each edge is examined once (twice if undirected), so BFS costs O(V + E) with adjacency lists.

BFS has a valuable property: it discovers each vertex by the path with the fewest edges, so recording each vertex’s parent when it is discovered yields shortest paths in an unweighted graph — the number of “hops”. It computes levels (distance from s), tests connectivity and bipartiteness (two-colourability), and powers “friends within three steps” queries. On the small graph A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D, D–E, BFS from A visits A B C D E: A first, then its neighbours B and C, then D, then E. The C++ program does the same on a matrix; the card animates the frontier.

Run BFS by hand on a small graph with a queue. In what order do the vertices leave the queue?
keynotes: BFS visits the start vertex, then all its neighbours, then all their unvisited neighbours, using a queue.
Marking a vertex when it is enqueued, not dequeued, prevents it from being added twice.
Each vertex enters the queue once and each edge is examined once, so the cost is O(V + E).

dfs.body:
Now imagine walking a maze with a ball of string, always taking a new corridor and backing up at dead ends: that is depth-first search. Depth-first search (DFS) explores as far as possible along one path before backing up — like walking a maze with a ball of string, always taking a new corridor and returning at a dead end. The code is recursion: mark u visited; for each neighbour v not yet visited, call DFS(v). The recursion stack is the stack ADT of Chapter 2 (an explicit stack gives an iterative version). The cost is the same O(V + E). From A on the same graph the order is A B D E C — A, then B, then B’s neighbour D, then D’s neighbour E (a dead end), then back to D, A, and C.

DFS discovers structure BFS does not. Run it from every unvisited vertex in turn and the number of times you start is the number of connected components. A back edge (an edge to an ancestor still being explored) reveals a cycle. Finishing times give a topological order of a DAG, and DFS is the engine behind strongly-connected-component algorithms and maze solving (backtracking). The programs show a matrix-based DFS and a component counter: a seven-vertex graph with edges 0–1, 1–2, 3–4 has four components ({0,1,2}, {3,4}, {5}, {6}).

Run DFS from A by hand on the example graph and compare your order with the one given.
keynotes: DFS explores as far as possible along one path before backing up; the code is recursion: mark u visited, then call DFS(v) for each unvisited neighbour v.
The recursion stack is the stack ADT of Chapter 2, and an explicit stack gives an iterative version.
The cost is the same O(V + E); from A the order is A B D E C.

mst.body:
Suppose you had to connect several towns with cable as cheaply as possible; you would soon discover that cycles waste money. Two famous recipes solve it, and both are greedy: they grow the answer by always taking the cheapest safe edge, which you will see is the only decision they ever make. You must connect n towns by roads (or computers by cable) as cheaply as possible. Each possible road has a cost. You need the towns to be connected and no more roads than necessary: a cycle contains a redundant edge. The cheapest answer is a minimum spanning tree (MST): a spanning tree — a tree containing all V vertices, hence V − 1 edges — whose total edge weight is the least possible. It exists for every connected weighted graph, and is unique if all weights are distinct. Applications include network design, clustering, and approximations for travelling-salesman-like problems.

Two greedy algorithms find it. Kruskal’s algorithm thinks in edges: sort all edges by weight and go through them in order; add an edge unless it would form a cycle (its two ends are already connected). The cycle test uses union–find (disjoint sets): each vertex starts in its own set; an edge is accepted if its ends are in different sets, and then the sets merge. Cost O(E log E) for the sort. Prim’s algorithm thinks in vertices: start from any vertex, and repeatedly add the cheapest edge that connects the tree so far to a vertex outside it — like Dijkstra but comparing edge weights rather than path lengths. With a priority queue it costs O(E log V).

Why does greedy work here? The cut property: for any split of the vertices into two groups, the lightest edge crossing the split belongs to some MST. Both algorithms only ever add such an edge, so they cannot go wrong. On the textbook graph (nine vertices, fourteen edges) both give total weight 37 using 8 edges (9 − 1 = 8). Step the cards: Kruskal marks the edges it rejects as cycle-formers, Prim grows from A.

Why does a spanning tree on V vertices have exactly V − 1 edges? Think about what an extra edge would create. Then pick Kruskal or Prim for a graph of your choice and carry it out on paper for two or three edges.
keynotes: A minimum spanning tree contains all V vertices, hence V − 1 edges, with the least possible total weight.
It exists for every connected weighted graph and is unique if all weights are distinct.
Applications include network design and clustering.

sp.body:
Your satnav solves this problem many times a day, and you can follow the same idea with a pencil. The idea is to spread outwards from the source, always finalising the closest unsettled place, so that you never have to revisit an answer once it is settled. A satnav must find the cheapest route from where you are to everywhere else. In an unweighted graph BFS does it. With weights — distances, times, tolls — we need Dijkstra’s algorithm (1959), valid when all weights are non-negative. Keep a tentative distance dist[v] for every vertex (0 for the source, ∞ for the rest). Repeat: pick the unsettled vertex u with the smallest tentative distance — it is now settled, its distance is final — and relax each outgoing edge (u, v, w): if dist[u] + w < dist[v], set dist[v] to it and remember u as v’s parent. After all vertices are settled, the parents trace the shortest-path tree back to the source.

Why is the settled distance final? When u has the smallest tentative distance among unsettled vertices, any other route to u must leave the settled set through some unsettled vertex, whose distance is already at least dist[u]; with non-negative edges the rest of that route cannot make it shorter. That argument breaks with a negative edge, and Dijkstra can then give wrong answers; Bellman–Ford handles negative weights by relaxing all edges V − 1 times in O(V·E), and detects negative cycles. With a simple array to find the minimum, Dijkstra costs O(V²); with a binary heap it costs O((V + E) log V). The card runs it on the textbook graph: from u, the shortest path to z is u→x→y→z of length 4. The C++ program runs the O(V²) array version on a five-vertex graph and prints the final distances 0 7 3 9 5.

Why does Dijkstra’s algorithm fail with negative weights? Try a small example to see the trap. Then run it on a small graph with three or four vertices and keep a table of tentative distances.
keynotes: In an unweighted graph BFS finds shortest paths; with weights we need Dijkstra’s algorithm (1959), valid when all weights are non-negative.
Keep a tentative distance dist[v] for every vertex, 0 for the source and ∞ for the rest.
Repeat: settle the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance and relax its outgoing edges.

allpairs.body:
Sometimes one source is not enough and you need a whole table of distances, such as flight costs between every pair of airports. Sometimes you need the shortest distance between every pair of vertices — a table of flight costs between all airports. Running Dijkstra from each vertex works, but the Floyd–Warshall algorithm does it with a compact triple loop and handles negative edges (but not negative cycles). Define d[i][j] as the shortest known distance from i to j, initially the edge weight (0 on the diagonal, ∞ if no edge). Then, for each possible intermediate vertex k in turn, ask whether going through k helps: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]). After k has taken every value, d holds the true shortest distances. Three nested loops over V: O(V³) time, O(V²) space. The order of the loops matters — k must be the outermost.

Replace min and + by OR and AND and the same loop computes transitive closure (Warshall’s algorithm): reach[i][j] = reach[i][j] OR (reach[i][k] AND reach[k][j]) — is there any path from i to j? The program runs Floyd–Warshall on a four-vertex directed graph; look at the first row: from vertex 0 the best route to vertex 2 is 5, via vertex 1 (3 + 2), and to vertex 3 is 6 (via 1 and 2).

Explain in one sentence what the triple loop asks for each intermediate vertex k.
keynotes: Floyd–Warshall finds the shortest distance between every pair of vertices with a compact triple loop and handles negative edges but not negative cycles.
d[i][j] starts as the edge weight (0 on the diagonal, ∞ if no edge).
For each intermediate vertex k it asks whether going through k helps: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]).

topo.body:
Getting dressed has constraints, socks before shoes, and you resolve them without thinking; a computer needs an algorithm to do the same. Getting dressed has constraints: socks before shoes, trousers before belt. A topological order of a directed acyclic graph lists all vertices so that for every edge u → v, u comes before v. It is the schedule for build systems (compile this file before that), course prerequisites, spreadsheet recalculation and task planning. It exists if and only if the graph has no directed cycle — a cycle of dependencies cannot be satisfied — and there may be many valid orders.

Kahn’s algorithm peels the graph: compute every vertex’s in-degree; put all vertices of in-degree 0 in a queue; repeatedly remove a vertex from the queue, output it, and decrement the in-degree of its successors, enqueuing any that reach 0. If the output has fewer vertices than the graph, the rest lie on a cycle. Cost O(V + E). The DFS-based alternative outputs vertices in reverse finishing order. For a→b, a→c, b→d, c→d one order is a b c d (a first because it has no prerequisite, d last because it needs both b and c; b and c may swap).

Why can a graph with a cycle of dependencies have no topological order? Think of two tasks that each wait for the other.
keynotes: A topological order of a directed acyclic graph lists all vertices so that for every edge u → v, u comes before v.
It exists if and only if the graph has no directed cycle, and there may be many valid orders.
It schedules build systems, course prerequisites, spreadsheet recalculation and task planning.

summary.body:
Let’s pull the chapter together in a short list you can use as a checklist.

  • A graph is vertices plus edges (directed/undirected, weighted); degrees sum to 2E; a tree is a connected acyclic graph with V − 1 edges.
  • Store sparse graphs as adjacency lists (V + E), dense ones as matrices (V²).
  • BFS (queue) gives fewest-edge paths; DFS (stack/recursion) gives components, cycles and topological order; both O(V + E).
  • MST: Kruskal (sort edges + union–find) or Prim (grow a tree), justified by the cut property.
  • Shortest paths: Dijkstra for non-negative weights (heap: O((V + E) log V)), Bellman–Ford for negatives, Floyd–Warshall for all pairs in O(V³).
  • Topological sort needs a DAG; Kahn’s algorithm detects cycles.

Which of these algorithms would you reach for on a road map with distances? Say why before you move on.
keynotes: A graph is vertices plus edges; degrees sum to 2E, and a tree is a connected acyclic graph with V − 1 edges.
Store sparse graphs as adjacency lists (V + E) and dense ones as matrices (V²); BFS and DFS are both O(V + E).
Shortest paths use Dijkstra for non-negative weights and Bellman–Ford for negative ones; MSTs use Kruskal or Prim.
